I've gathered substantial material from Enduring Word, Precept Austin, Gill, Ellicott, and excerpts from Spurgeon, Keil & Delitzsch, Wiersbe, Constable, and others. Let me now compile the verse-by-verse notes. I wasn't able to search specifically for Catholic, Orthodox, or the "Daniel/Danel" scholarly debate due to search limits, so those will be noted as unfound.

---

## Ezekiel 14 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — "Then some of the elders of Israel came and sat down before me."

These "elders" (Hebrew *zaqen*, meaning community leaders) were leaders among the exiles in Babylon. They had visited Ezekiel before (Ezekiel 8:1). They came and sat before him, likely hoping for a prophetic oracle—perhaps about the length of the exile or news from Jerusalem. Their posture was outwardly respectful—silent, attentive, seemingly reverent—but as v. 3 reveals, their hearts were far from God.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/14.htm (Gill notes they came "to consult the Lord" by the prophet)
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_141-11 (notes the Hebrew *zaqen* and the leaders' failure to learn from Ezekiel's repeated warnings)

### v. 2 — "And the word of the LORD came to me, saying..."

Before the elders could state their errand, God preempted them by giving Ezekiel supernatural revelation about their hearts. This demonstrates that God knows all hidden things and that true prophecy originates with God, not with human inquiry.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/14.htm ("while the elders were sitting before him, and whispered secretly and powerfully the following things")

### v. 3 — "Son of man, these men have set up idols in their hearts and put wicked stumbling blocks before their faces. Should I consult with them in any way?"

**"Idols in their hearts"** — Unlike the blatant, open idolatry in Jerusalem (Ezekiel 8), these exiles practiced a *secret idolatry of the heart*. They had no physical images in Babylon, but in their affections and thoughts they had enthroned other gods. Gill notes the Hebrew word for idols (*gillulim*) carries the sense of "dunghill gods"—filthy and worthless things. This internal idolatry was invisible to others but fully seen by God.

**"Stumbling block of their iniquity"** — Their idolatry was a trap that would cause them to fall into sin and ultimately into judgment. Precept Austin notes that "stumbling block" (*mikshowl*) is used 14 times in the OT, 8 in Ezekiel, and represents something that trips a person up into moral and physical ruin.

**"Should I be inquired of at all by them?"** — The implied answer is a forceful "No." This rhetorical question parallels Psalm 66:18 ("If I regard wickedness in my heart, the Lord will not hear"). God refuses to be consulted by hypocrites.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/ (Guzik: compares these elders to the Pharisees Jesus rebuked in Matthew 15:8–9)
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/14.htm (explains "dunghill gods" etymology and the affront of consulting God with a divided heart)
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_141-11 (Wiersbe: "They pretended to be spiritual by inquiring of Ezekiel, but God saw their hearts")
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/14.htm (Ellicott: "it was idle to imagine He would allow Himself to be enquired of by them")

### v. 4 — "Therefore speak to them and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: 'When any Israelite sets up idols in his heart and puts a wicked stumbling block before his face, and then comes to the prophet, I the LORD will answer him according to his great idolatry...'"

God commands Ezekiel to answer, but not with the oracle the elders hoped for. Instead, God Himself will answer—not with words of guidance but with an answer "according to the multitude of his idols"—that is, an answer of judgment proportionate to their idolatry. Ellicott points out that the Hebrew verb for "answer" here is passive/reflexive: "I will show myself answering," a softer but ominous form. The principle is that when a person's heart is not submissive to God, God will allow him to be deceived (Balaam, Numbers 22:20; Micaiah, 1 Kings 22:15).
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/14.htm ("No man can hope to know what God would have him to do unless his own heart is truly submissive")
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/14.htm (Gill: God would answer "not in a way of grace and mercy, but in a way of judgment")

### v. 5 — "...so that I may take hold of the hearts of the people of Israel. For because of their idols, they are all estranged from Me."

**"Take hold of the hearts"** — The Hebrew verb conveys a forceful, even violent seizing—like capturing prisoners (1 Samuel 15:8), conquering a city (Deuteronomy 20:19), or parents seizing a rebellious son (Deuteronomy 21:19). Guzik explains that God intended through judgment to "recapture" the alienated hearts of His people. Gill offers an alternative reading from the Targum: "that I may bring near the house of Israel, and put repentance into their hearts."

**"Estranged from Me"** — The Hebrew *zur* can also mean "commit adultery." Precept Austin notes this spiritual adultery language: Israel, as God's "wife" (cf. Isaiah 54:5), committed adultery by seeking other gods. The Pulpit Commentary adds that sinners "shall be taken in the snare which they have made for themselves."
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_141-11 (on *zur* meaning "commit adultery")
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/14.htm (Gill on the Targum interpretation)
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/14-5.htm (Pulpit Commentary on v. 5)

### v. 6 — "Therefore tell the house of Israel that this is what the Lord GOD says: 'Repent and turn away from your idols; turn your faces away from all your abominations.'"

The only proper answer to such inquirers is a call to repentance. God defines repentance concretely: turning away from idols and abominations. Ellicott stresses that "the only repentance acceptable to Him is that which has its seat in the affections of the heart"—not mere outward reformation. Gill notes the Hebrew construction suggests not only turning oneself but also causing others to turn: "turn, and cause to be turned from your idols." Whedon adds: "The Lord will give to these idolaters no view of the future until they pluck their idols out of their hearts."
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/14.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/14.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/ezekiel-14.html (Whedon)

### v. 7 — "For when any Israelite or any foreigner dwelling in Israel separates himself from Me, sets up idols in his heart, and puts a wicked stumbling block before his face, and then comes to the prophet to inquire of Me, I the LORD will answer him Myself."

The warning is broadened to include both native Israelites and resident foreigners (*gerim*). Under the Mosaic theocracy, foreigners living in the land were bound to respect the law against idolatry (Leviticus 17:10; 20:1-2). The key accusation is not outward idolatry but the hypocrisy of combining secret devotion to idols with outward inquiry of Yahweh. God will answer "by Myself"—not through the prophet, but by directly intervening in judgment.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/14.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/ (citing Vawter and Hoppe: all have "cut themselves off from Yahweh's prophetic communication")
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_141-11 (Charles Dyer: "God was not obligated to answer them when they refused to acknowledge His sovereignty")

### v. 8 — "I will set My face against that man and make him a sign and a proverb; I will cut him off from among My people. Then you will know that I am the LORD."

**"Set My face against that man"** — A fearsome idiom meaning God will personally oppose him with focused attention. Trapp (cited by Guzik) says: "I will look him to death."

**"A sign and a proverb"** — The judgment would be so severe that the man would become a byword—a proverbial example of divine wrath. Block (cited by Guzik) compares this to "Nimrod" (proverbial for hunting) and "Babel" (for confusion). Ellicott prefers the Hebrew text rendering: "will make him desolate for a sign and a proverb." The language echoes covenant curses in Deuteronomy 28:37 and Leviticus 20:3, 5-6.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/14.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/14.htm (Gill: "a spectacle of horror... because of his misery")

### v. 9 — "But if the prophet is enticed to speak a message, then it was I the LORD who enticed him, and I will stretch out My hand against him and destroy him from among My people Israel."

This is the most theologically difficult verse in the chapter. The statement that God "enticed" (or "deceived") the false prophet must be understood carefully. The consensus among the commentators I read is that this is not God actively creating deception *ex nihilo*, but God giving sinners over to the consequences of their own sinful choices—what Ellicott calls "the natural consequence of the immutable moral laws which He has ordained."

Gill explicitly connects this to 1 Kings 22:22 (the lying spirit sent to Ahab's prophets) and 2 Thessalonians 2:11 ("God sends them a strong delusion"). He argues that while God is not the author of sin, He wills it to be done for wise purposes, sometimes as judgment for prior sin. Ellicott explains: "God does not force men either to receive the truth or to act righteously. If, notwithstanding His remonstrances, their hearts are set upon wrong, He will even give them up."

Guzik (Enduring Word), citing Block, puts it bluntly: "Yahweh answers insincerity with insincerity. Unrepentant kings and unrepentant people... do not deserve a straight answer." Feinberg adds: "When the false prophet, sensing the desires of his idolatrous inquirers, gave them... a prophetic word in keeping with their wishes... ultimately it was the Lord who had enticed him. There is an elimination of secondary causes as in Isaiah 45:7 and Amos 3:6." Trapp says: "I had not only a permissive, but an active hand in that imposture; not as a sin, but as a punishment of other sins."

**Reformed emphasis (seen in Guzik/Enduring Word, which is broadly Reformed-Baptist):** God's sovereignty extends even over false prophecy—He ordains the deception as a judicial hardening, while the false prophet remains fully culpable.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/14.htm (extensive treatment—this is the most detailed source)
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/14.htm

### v. 10 — "They will bear their punishment—the punishment of the inquirer will be the same as that of the prophet—"

Both the false prophet and the idolatrous inquirer are equally guilty and will share the same punishment. Neither can excuse the other. Precept Austin summarizes: "God is saying that both are fully culpable for their bad choices and will suffer the consequences thereof. God is not being unfair." Poole (cited by Guzik) says it is "hard to say whose sin is greatest." Trapp adds: "Neither shall excuse other; but as they have sinned together, so shall they suffer together."
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_141-11
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/14.htm (both were "alike culpable, each pursuing the desires of their own evil hearts")

### v. 11 — "...in order that the house of Israel may no longer stray from Me and no longer defile themselves with all their transgressions. Then they will be My people and I will be their God, declares the Lord GOD."

The ultimate purpose of judgment is redemptive—to stop Israel's straying, to purify them, and to restore the covenant relationship ("My people... their God"). This is the covenant formula repeated throughout Scripture (cf. Leviticus 26:12; Jeremiah 31:33). Historically, this was fulfilled: after the Babylonian exile, Israel was largely cured of idolatry.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/ (Guzik: "When Israel came back into the land in the days of Ezra and Nehemiah, they did not have the same problem with idolatry as before")
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/14.htm ("the object of all the previous severity of judgment—that Israel may be brought to a true repentance")

### vv. 12-20 — The Second Oracle: Four Judgments and the Inefficacy of Intercessory Righteousness

This section forms a unified rhetorical argument. The people evidently hoped that Jerusalem would be spared for the sake of the righteous within it—as God had promised Abraham regarding Sodom (Genesis 18:23-32). God systematically demolishes this hope by listing four judgments, each time repeating that even the three most righteous men imaginable could save only themselves.

**The four judgments** (famine, wild beasts, sword, pestilence) all echo the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 (vv. 22, 25-26) and correspond to the "four horsemen" imagery in Revelation 6:1-8.

**Why Noah, Daniel, and Job?** Ellicott gives the most thorough answer: all three were not only eminently holy but had been instruments in saving others—Noah saved his family (Genesis 6:18), Daniel saved his companions and the wise men of Chaldea (Daniel 2:17-18), and Job's intercession saved his friends (Job 42:7-8). Yet even their combined intercession would not avert national judgment. Gill adds that Daniel, though a young man (about 30) at this time, was already famous for his piety—placed between the ancient patriarchs Noah and Job. The inclusion of a contemporary (Daniel) alongside ancient figures emphasizes that no one—past or present—could intercede successfully.

*Regarding the scholarly debate about whether "Daniel" refers to the biblical Daniel or a legendary Ugaritic figure "Danel": modern critical scholars sometimes argue for the latter, but this was not found in the sources I could access from the permitted sites.*
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/14.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/14.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-14.html (Keil & Delitzsch overview)

### vv. 12-14 — Famine
God declares that even Noah, Daniel, and Job could deliver only themselves by their righteousness if famine struck the land. The "staff of bread" (v. 13) is a metaphor for the food supply that sustains life (cf. Ezekiel 4:16). Adam Clarke (cited by Guzik): "Noah, though a righteous man, could not by his intercession preserve the old world from being drowned. Job... could not preserve his children... Daniel... could not prevent the captivity of his country."
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/14.htm

### vv. 15-16 — Wild Beasts
The second judgment repeats the same formula. When Babylon depopulated the land, wild animals multiplied and made life dangerous (cf. Deuteronomy 7:22, where God had promised to drive out Canaanites "little by little" lest wild beasts overrun the land). Notably, the statement is strengthened: "they could not deliver their own sons or daughters"—not even their immediate family.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-14.html (Keil & Delitzsch: the judgments are from Leviticus 26)

### vv. 17-18 — The Sword
The third judgment: invading armies. Again, the three righteous men could not deliver even sons or daughters. Guzik notes the repeated oath formula "as I live" (also in vv. 16, 20) strengthens the certainty of the declaration.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/

### vv. 19-20 — Plague/Pestilence
The fourth judgment. The "four horsemen" parallel to Revelation 6:1-8 is noted by Guzik and Wiersbe. The formula "they would deliver only themselves by their righteousness" is repeated for emphasis.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_141-11 (Wiersbe)

---

### v. 21 — "For this is what the Lord GOD says: 'How much worse will it be when I send against Jerusalem My four dire judgments—sword, famine, wild beasts, and plague—in order to cut off from it both man and beast?'"

This is the climax (*a fortiori* argument): if any one of these judgments alone would be unstoppable even by the holiest intercessors, how much more when all four are unleashed together upon Jerusalem! The rhetorical question intensifies the certainty and severity of the coming judgment.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/14.htm ("The teaching of the preceding eight verses is here gathered up into its climax")

### v. 22 — "Yet, behold, some survivors will be left in it—sons and daughters who will be brought out. They will come out to you, and when you see their conduct and actions, you will be comforted regarding the disaster I have brought upon Jerusalem—all that I have brought upon it."

This is a surprising twist. There *will* be a remnant—but not a righteous one. The phrase "their conduct and actions" (literally "their ways and their doings") almost always carries a negative connotation in Ezekiel. Taylor (cited by Guzik) states that "most recent commentators recognize that the context demands that these words refer to 'unrighteous doings.'" These survivors would be so wicked that when the exiles in Babylon saw their behavior, they would be "comforted"—not in the sense of feeling better, but in the sense of being convinced that God's judgment was entirely just. Ellicott explains: "when you see the wickedness of this remnant, you will cease to mourn over the judgment, for you cannot but perceive that it was a righteous act of God."
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/14.htm

### v. 23 — "They will bring you consolation when you see their conduct and actions, and you will know that it was not without cause that I have done all these things within it,' declares the Lord GOD."

The final note of the chapter is the vindication of God's justice. The wickedness of the survivors provides visible proof that God did nothing "without cause" (or "in vain," as the margin reads). F.B. Meyer (cited by Precept Austin) reflects: "We do not know the cause of so much that crushes us to the ground. But if we did know it as well as we shall know it some day, we should have no difficulty in reconciling God's dealings with his perfect love."
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel-f_b_meyer (F.B. Meyer on v. 23)

## Distinctive Protestant Tradition Emphases

### Baptist / Spurgeon (from spurgeon.org)
Spurgeon's sermon "A Delusion Dispelled" focuses on **individual responsibility**: "In all the procedures of divine judgment the principle of individual responsibility can never be relaxed. Hence the need of personal piety—the absolute necessity that men and women should pray for themselves—that each one should repent for himself, that each one should believe for himself, and that each one should in his own proper person be born again." He strongly denounces sponsorship ("sponsors in religion are a wicked superstition") and any idea that another's righteousness can cover one's sin. He emphasizes that Noah, Daniel, and Job could not intercede successfully for the ungodly, and that "the prayers of the greatest intercessors cannot avail if men persist in their unbelief."
- https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/a-delusion-dispelled

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word)
David Guzik (Enduring Word, a broadly charismatic-leaning commentary) emphasizes the **application to contemporary believers**: examining one's heart for hidden idols, the principle that "no one can shelter under another's goodness," and the call to be "born again for themselves." He brings the chapter into personal devotional application, citing modern illustrations (J. Yoder's story about materialism as idolatry, Paul Azinger's cancer leading him to reorder priorities). The treatment is less academic and more pastoral-practical.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-14/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_141-11 (extensive devotional illustrations)

### Reformed (Keil & Delitzsch, Ellicott)
These commentators emphasize the **covenantal and theological structure**: the four judgments as echoing Leviticus 26 covenant curses, the parallel with Jeremiah 15:1 (where Moses and Samuel are named instead), and the careful theological explanation of how God "deceives" the prophet (divine judicial hardening). Ellicott's treatment of v. 9 is the most philosophically careful: God "persuades" the prophet "in the same sense in which He hardened Pharaoh's heart, by making such persuasion the natural consequence of the immutable moral laws which He has ordained."
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/14.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-14.html
